content_selection.rationale: Most of the major stories made it in: the AI-debt and CoreWeave credit stress, CERT-In's report on AI agents, the Beam open weights, and China's AI export controls. Repeats from earlier briefs and marketing posts were also cut sensibly. But the brief missed at least one widely covered story because the article was never opened: Meta's new commercial terms, which let it crawl business customers' websites and train AI on the content. It also cut Anthropic's METR evaluator-access announcement, which Reuters, CNBC and TechCrunch covered, while running an older Anthropic post (the midterms safeguards) and a low-value AWS vendor blog about agent evaluation. China's export-control proposal was underplayed: it ran only as a headline item, but it is a major policy story with a 2-trillion-parameter threshold and an export registration rule already in effect.
content_selection.evidence: Candidate list: "[excluded] Meta grants itself right to scrape business customer content for training (headline only; article not opened)" and "[excluded] Anthropic: an update on independent evaluators (METR employee-level access, 2026-10-15)", while "[included] AWS SMGS nine-stage agent evaluation framework on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (MTTD under four hours, company-reported)".

selection_disagreements.story: Meta grants itself right to scrape/crawl business customers' websites for AI training (new Commercial Terms effective Oct 30)
selection_disagreements.rationale: Several outlets covered this widely: The Register, Nieman Lab, Ars Technica and trade press. Cornell's James Grimmelmann said the terms clearly permit training on publisher sites, and the News/Media Alliance CEO called the policy "outrageous and probably illegal." There is no opt-out for business customers, and The Register notes at least a million businesses use Meta's AI agents in WhatsApp and Messenger alone. It is a significant data-rights story, and it was dropped only because the article wasn't opened.

selection_disagreements.story: Anthropic gives METR employee-like access as an independent evaluator (Oct 15)
selection_disagreements.rationale: Reuters, CNBC, TechCrunch and others covered it. Six METR staff are embedded with access roughly on par with Anthropic's internal risk teams, METR can publish without an Anthropic veto, and the move ties to the White House accord on independent evaluators. It is unclear from the candidate list whether it ran in the Oct 16 brief; it isn't marked as covered. Either way, it is a more substantive safety-governance story than the Oct 14 midterms post that was included.

selection_disagreements.story: AWS SMGS nine-stage agent evaluation framework on Bedrock AgentCore
selection_disagreements.rationale: This is an internal vendor how-to blog post with company-reported metrics and illustrative dashboard numbers. The brief itself flags those caveats. It has little news value compared with the excluded Meta terms and METR stories.

factual_accuracy.rationale: I checked most of the brief's specific claims against primary sources: Axios (both articles), TechCrunch, Reflection AI, Microsoft Research, arXiv, Anthropic, Google Research, the NVIDIA newsroom, Vercel's index, AP coverage of China's export controls, and the coverage of PostgreSQL, Replit, Elorian and Muse Spark. Nearly every number, quote and attribution matched the sources, including the 1,100bp CDS figure, the $7T vs $3.6T Gartner comparison, the Athanor scores, the Magnetar speedups, Anthropic's usage percentages, the aptamer specificity figures, Beam's benchmarks and the 23-of-40 export-control items. The brief also labeled vendor-reported and single-preprint results as such. The only problems were small: the arXiv paper was submitted October 15, not 16; the brief gives Jev's spend share as 0.15% (The Register's number) while Vercel itself says 0.27% over Jev's first two weeks; secondary sources disagree on Elorian's valuation; and I could not check the AWS AgentCore post.
factual_accuracy.evidence: The brief says CoreWeave's "five-year credit default swaps near 1,100 basis points on Thursday, roughly $1.1 million a year to insure $10 million of its debt." Axios gives the same figures: "nearly 1,100 basis points" and "about $1.1 million a year to insure $10 million of CoreWeave bonds."

length_format.rationale: The counts are within the stated ranges: there are 15 Headlines bullets (the top of the 8-15 range) and 7 deep-dives (Research 3, Products 1, Industry 1, Policy 2), and the empty Benchmarks section is correctly omitted. However, every deep-dive overshoots the 3-6 sentence target, typically running 8-11 sentences, and the CoreWeave item is especially long. The brief also adds an unstated 'Headline-only items' section with multi-sentence summaries, which adds bulk beyond the specified structure. Count and structure compliance is good, but per-item length is systematically out of spec.
length_format.evidence: The CoreWeave deep-dive runs about 11 sentences, from 'The 2026-10-15 brief noted that the chip sell-off...' through the Gil Luria 'subprime tranche' quote. The Google wet-lab item is about 9-10 sentences, against a 3-6 sentence target.

dedup.rationale: Most of today's stories are new and absent from the 10-14, 10-15 and 10-16 editions, including Beam, Magnetar, Athanor, the Google wet lab, Anthropic's midterm safeguards, Glimpse, PostgreSQL 19, Replit, NVIDIA UK, Vercel, AWS evaluation and China's export controls. The CoreWeave credit item is clearly labelled as a follow-up to the 10-15 sell-off and adds substantial new data, so it is justified. India's CERT-In report is a distinct new event, flagged only as 'Related.' The Apple–Meta Muse Spark Open item is labelled as a follow-up, but its core fact (Muse Spark Open runs on linked M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX, under a commercial-use license) was already the 10-16 lead, and it adds only thin new detail, so it is a minor, headline-only dedup weakness.
dedup.evidence: Today: 'Apple and Meta worked for several months to run Muse Spark Open locally across two or four connected M5 Ultra Mac Studios using Apple's MLX framework.' 10-16: 'The showcase setup is two M5 Ultra Mac Studios ... linked to run the model through Apple's MLX framework.'
